title: How Humans Build on Each Other: Cumulative Culture and Recursive Self-Improvement
length_note: Nine classes are needed. Class 1 introduces the core idea (the ratchet). Class 2 explains why humans are built to learn from each other. Classes 3 to 7 follow the transmission technologies in the order they appeared: speech, writing, printing and schools, science, then the internet and AI. Class 8 covers how knowledge is lost, which only makes sense once the learner knows how it is kept. Class 9 covers the extended mind and pulls the course together. Seven topics would leave out printing/schools or the loss of knowledge, and more than nine would repeat material. Each class is 30 to 45 minutes. The shorter ones suit tired learners, including adults relearning after a brain injury. The longer ones are the classes with the most to cover (science, internet and AI, and the extended mind). Every class has a recap, one main idea at a time, and a short 'try it' activity, so learners can stop at any break and still have something whole. Each class also ties to the history-of-everything timeline with one 'where are we on the timeline?' step.

classes.title: The Ratchet: What Cumulative Culture Is
classes.goal: Explain in plain words how each generation can start where the last one stopped, and give one example of an invention that no single person could have made alone.
topics: The cultural ratchet: gaining knowledge and not slipping back
Cumulative culture versus ordinary culture and individual cleverness
Why one person alone cannot reinvent a smartphone, or even a pencil
Teaching and copying as the 'clicks' of the ratchet
Course overview: transmission, learning to learn, loss, extended mind
Timeline: placing the course on the history-of-everything timeline, from early humans to now

classes.title: Built to Learn From Others: Gene-Culture Coevolution
classes.goal: Describe how culture and genes shaped each other, using at least two examples, and say why this made humans such strong social learners.
topics: Gene-culture coevolution defined simply
Examples: fire and cooking, milk digestion in some populations, others to be verified
Why humans copy so faithfully, including over-imitation and teaching
Social learning compared with other animals, with care about what is and isn't settled
Where the evidence is strong and where scientists still disagree
Timeline: control of fire, the growth of the human brain, the spread of farming and herding

classes.title: Speech: The First Great Handing-Down
classes.goal: Explain how spoken language and storytelling let knowledge pass between generations, and name one strength and one weakness of memory-only transmission.
topics: Language as a way to share what you know, not only what you see
Oral traditions, songs, rhythm and story as memory aids
Apprenticeship: learning by watching and doing alongside speaking
The limits of memory: drift, forgetting, group size
What scientists do and don't know about when language began
Timeline: the origin of language and early modern humans

classes.title: Writing: Memory Outside the Head
classes.goal: Say how writing changed what could be stored and shared, and describe one thing it made easier and one thing it made harder.
topics: From tallies and tokens to writing systems
Records, laws, accounts, letters and libraries
Knowledge that can travel across distance and wait across time
Who could read and write, and who was left out
Trade-offs: memory skills versus stored records, kept balanced and evidence-based
Timeline: the first writing systems and early cities

classes.title: Printing and Schools: Copying at Scale
classes.goal: Explain how printing and organised schooling made knowledge cheaper and more widely shared, and connect this to the idea of the ratchet.
topics: Hand copying versus printing: speed, cost and errors
Woodblock and movable-type printing, and the spread of the press
The printing house as a workplace: craft, trade and knowledge, with link to the earlier Blake class to be checked
Schools, universities and literacy as ways of passing on learning
Standard texts, shared references and the spread of ideas, both good and bad
Timeline: early printing in East Asia, the press in Europe, the rise of mass schooling

classes.title: Science: A Method That Improves the Methods
classes.goal: Explain how science checks and corrects knowledge, and describe how better tools and better methods of learning have sped up learning itself.
topics: Learning how to learn: methods that improve how we learn
Science as organised testing, sharing, checking and correcting
Peer review, replication, journals and citation as a shared memory
Tools that made new tools: telescopes, microscopes, instruments, computers
Feedback loops: what 'recursive' means in everyday terms, using the improvement of improvement
Study methods people can use, such as spacing, practice and teaching others, kept evidence-based
Timeline: the scientific revolution, the Industrial Revolution and modern research

classes.title: The Internet and AI: Fast Copying, New Learners
classes.goal: Describe how the internet and AI change the sharing of knowledge, and say clearly what is known and what is only speculation about AI improving itself.
topics: The internet: near-instant sharing, search, open knowledge, and the problem of misinformation
How to check a source in a few simple steps
What AI systems are, in plain words, and how they are trained on human-made text, images and code
AI as a tool for learning, and its limits and errors
What 'recursive self-improvement' means in AI discussions, and the difference between present facts and predictions
Who gets to take part: access, language, cost and disability
Timeline: the personal computer, the web, and recent AI, with dates verified

classes.title: How Knowledge Gets Lost
classes.goal: Give three ways knowledge can be lost, and name one practical step that helps keep knowledge alive.
topics: Loss through broken chains: fewer teachers, small groups, war, disaster
Loss through format change: unreadable scripts, old files, dead media
Loss through neglect or suppression
Famous stories checked for accuracy, sorting well-supported cases from myths and debated claims
Fragility of digital records and the work of archives and preservation
Forgetting in one person's life, and how notes, routines and other people help
Timeline: lost and rediscovered knowledge across the eras covered so far

classes.title: The Extended Mind: Tools as Part of How We Think
classes.goal: Explain the extended mind idea in plain words, give an example from daily life, and sum up how all the classes fit together.
topics: The extended mind idea: notebooks, phones, maps and calendars as part of thinking, and the debate around it
Everyday tools that support memory and attention, including assistive technology
Dependence and independence: choosing tools wisely and keeping skills that matter to you
Culture as a shared extended mind that reaches across generations
Putting it together: the ratchet, the transmission tools, learning to learn, loss, and the extended mind
A personal project: one thing I know, who taught me, and how I could pass it on
Timeline: a final walk through the whole course, from fire to AI
